title: As: Simultaneous Events and Reasons
summary: Use as to connect events happening together, actions in progress, parallel changes and background reasons. Distinguish temporal as from causal as, and choose when instead for events described as following one another.
learningObjectives: Link actions occurring at the same time using as followed by a complete clause.
Describe an event happening during an ongoing activity and mark an exact coincidence with just as.
Use as for two changes developing together over a period of time.
Identify when as means because rather than at the same time as.
Use when for a later or single-time event when simultaneous action is not intended.

explanation.heading: As connects actions that overlap in time
explanation.body: Use as + subject + verb when two things happen together. One action may be brief, such as a person waving, while another unfolds, such as a vehicle moving away. As draws attention to the overlap, not simply the order of events. The clauses can appear in either order without changing the basic simultaneous meaning.
explanation.example: As the audience took their seats, a pianist played quietly near the entrance.

explanation.heading: An event during an ongoing action
explanation.body: As can introduce an action already in progress when something else happens. Past continuous often makes the ongoing background clear: as someone was carrying equipment, a new event interrupted them. The clause introduced by as provides the time setting rather than the reason for the second event.
explanation.example: A shelf collapsed as we were moving the boxes into storage.

explanation.heading: Just as marks an exact moment
explanation.body: Just as adds emphasis to a precise point of overlap: something happens at the exact moment another event begins or ends. This can make an interruption sound unexpected or particularly well timed. Just as is stronger than as alone when the timing itself is the important detail.
explanation.example: Just as the presenter opened the slideshow, the projector stopped working.

explanation.heading: As describes changes unfolding together
explanation.body: Use as when two situations develop over the same period. The link may describe parallel changes rather than a single instant. Words such as gradually, more, less and increasingly often appear in one of the clauses because the speaker is tracking how things change together.
explanation.example: As the weeks passed, the new volunteers became more confident.

explanation.heading: As can give a reason; when can locate a time
explanation.body: As can also mean because and introduce a reason that helps explain the main clause. Context shows whether the connection is causal or temporal. Compare As the restaurant was full, we chose another place (reason) with As we walked past the restaurant, we saw its new sign (simultaneous actions). When can simply identify a time or period, especially when one event happens after another. If you only mean at that time in someone’s life, when is usually clearer.
explanation.example: As the last bus had already left, we shared a taxi home.

comparisons.title: Simultaneous activity versus a later action

left.label: As: during the activity
left.example: As I crossed the courtyard, I heard the church bells.
left.note: The sound happened while the crossing was underway.

right.label: When: after arrival
right.example: When I reached the office, I opened my laptop.
right.note: The first event reaches its endpoint before the next action begins.

left.label: As = while
left.example: As the children painted, their teacher arranged the materials.
left.note: The painting and preparation happened at the same time.

right.label: As = because
right.example: As the paint was still wet, the teacher moved the artwork carefully.
right.note: The wet paint explains why the artwork was handled with care.

left.label: As
left.example: As the guests chatted, the host brought out snacks.
left.note: The activities overlap for part of their duration.

right.label: Just as
right.example: Just as the host served dessert, the lights went out.
right.note: The interruption occurred at that particular moment.

examples.sentence: A child waved to us as the ferry pulled away from the pier.
examples.note: Both actions happened together at departure.

examples.sentence: My phone rang as I was searching for the booking reference.
examples.note: The brief call began during the ongoing search.

examples.sentence: Just as the referee raised her whistle, the crowd fell silent.
examples.note: Just as emphasizes a precise shared moment.

examples.sentence: As the concert went on, the musicians seemed more relaxed.
examples.note: The change in confidence developed over the duration of the concert.

examples.sentence: As there were no empty tables, we ordered our drinks to take away.
examples.note: As supplies the cause of the decision, not a time relationship.

examples.sentence: When I was fifteen, I spent a summer learning to sail.
examples.note: When locates the period of life; as might misleadingly introduce a reason.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Just as I was leaving, the bus will arrive.
commonMistakes.correct: Just as I was leaving, the bus arrived.
commonMistakes.why: Keep the same past-time viewpoint for the two linked events.

commonMistakes.incorrect: As I was twelve, I joined the school orchestra.
commonMistakes.correct: When I was twelve, I joined the school orchestra.
commonMistakes.why: When identifies an age or period of life; as could suggest because of that age.

commonMistakes.incorrect: As I was carrying the tray, I was drop it.
commonMistakes.correct: As I was carrying the tray, I dropped it.
commonMistakes.why: The ongoing background uses was carrying, while the brief event uses the past simple dropped.

commonMistakes.incorrect: As the station was closed, so we took a taxi.
commonMistakes.correct: As the station was closed, we took a taxi.
commonMistakes.why: As already introduces the reason; do not insert so before the main clause in this structure.

studyTips: For each as-clause, ask whether it answers when (overlap) or why (reason), and underline the context that proves your choice.
Practise building paired timelines: as for overlapping actions, just as for a precise shared instant, and when for a later event.
Compare a growing trend with its parallel change: As X increased, Y decreased; then practise a separate causal example using as meaning because.

exercises.prompt: A colleague was filing reports while another employee was checking receipts. Which sentence highlights that the actions overlapped?
choices: As Maya filed the reports, Ben checked the receipts.
As Maya had filed the reports, Ben checked the receipts afterwards.
When Maya finished filing, Ben started checking receipts.
exercises.feedback: As with two activities in progress expresses their overlap; the other choices place one action after another.

exercises.prompt: The printer failed at the exact moment the technician pressed Start. Choose the expression that emphasizes the precise timing.
choices: Because the technician pressed Start, the printer failed.
Just as the technician pressed Start, the printer failed.
After the technician went home, the printer failed.
exercises.feedback: Just as expresses exact coincidence without claiming that pressing Start caused the failure.

exercises.prompt: The organisers cancelled the outdoor film because the screen was damaged. Which sentence uses as for that reason?
choices: As the screen was being carried, the organisers cancelled the film.
When the screen was damaged, the organisers cancelled the film.
As the screen was damaged, the organisers cancelled the film.
exercises.feedback: Here as introduces the damaged screen as the reason for cancellation; the other choices foreground timing.

exercises.prompt: The speaker means that they cooked dinner only after reaching home, not during the journey. Which sentence is clearest?
choices: When I got home, I cooked dinner.
As I was travelling home, I cooked dinner.
Just as I was driving home, I cooked dinner.
exercises.feedback: When identifies the completed arrival as the time before dinner preparation; as would suggest overlap.

exercises.prompt: ___ I was arranging the chairs, the first guests entered the hall. (use as to link simultaneous events)
exercises.feedback: As introduces the background activity that was happening when the guests entered.

exercises.prompt: Just ___ I opened the door, the alarm began to sound. (complete the expression for exact coincidence)
exercises.feedback: Just as marks the precise moment when the alarm started.

exercises.prompt: ___ the afternoon went on, the shadows became longer. (use as for two developments over time)
exercises.feedback: As links the passage of time with a developing change in the shadows.

exercises.prompt: ___ the museum was closed for repairs, we visited the gardens instead. (use as to introduce a reason)
exercises.feedback: As means because here; the closure explains the choice of another destination.

exercises.prompt: Correct the missing word in the expression for exact coincidence: The applause began just the singer finished the last note.
acceptedAnswers: The applause began just as the singer finished the last note.
exercises.feedback: Just as introduces the precise moment when the applause began.

exercises.prompt: Correct the missing verb in this background action: As we leaving the concert, we saw an old friend.
acceptedAnswers: As we were leaving the concert, we saw an old friend.
exercises.feedback: Were leaving gives the ongoing action during which the meeting occurred.

exercises.prompt: Keep the account in the past. Correct only the final verb form: As the evening went on, the air becomes cooler.
acceptedAnswers: As the evening went on, the air became cooler.
exercises.feedback: Became agrees with went and describes the gradual change during that evening.

exercises.prompt: Remove the unnecessary linking word: As the bridge was closed, so the drivers used another route.
acceptedAnswers: As the bridge was closed, the drivers used another route.
exercises.feedback: As already links the reason to the result, so a second so is unnecessary.

speakingExercises.prompt: Two actions happened together: the passengers entered the train; an announcement played. Begin with "As the passengers" and use the past simple in both clauses.
acceptedAnswers: As the passengers entered the train, an announcement played.
speakingExercises.feedback: As connects the announcement to the passengers entering at the same time.

speakingExercises.prompt: A brief event occurred during a longer one: I was packing my bag; the phone rang. Begin "The phone rang" and use "as I was packing my bag".
acceptedAnswers: The phone rang as I was packing my bag.
speakingExercises.feedback: As I was packing gives the ongoing action during which the phone rang.

speakingExercises.prompt: The lights failed at the exact moment the show began. Begin "Just as the show began" and end with "the lights failed".
acceptedAnswers: Just as the show began, the lights failed.
speakingExercises.feedback: Just as highlights the exact shared moment.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express parallel development. Facts: the weeks passed; the trainees grew more confident. Begin "As the weeks passed".
acceptedAnswers: As the weeks passed, the trainees grew more confident.
speakingExercises.feedback: As introduces a changing time frame during which confidence increased.

speakingExercises.prompt: Explain why the class moved indoors: it was raining heavily. Begin "As it was raining heavily" and finish with "we moved the class indoors".
acceptedAnswers: As it was raining heavily, we moved the class indoors.
speakingExercises.feedback: As means because here, explaining the move.

speakingExercises.prompt: State the time in someone’s life, not a reason. Facts: I was fourteen; I joined a choir. Begin "When I was fourteen".
acceptedAnswers: When I was fourteen, I joined a choir.
speakingExercises.feedback: When unambiguously identifies a period of life.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences. First: you were checking the timetable while the bus arrived; begin "As I was checking the timetable". Second: there were no seats, so you stood; begin "As there were no seats".
acceptedAnswers: As I was checking the timetable, the bus arrived. As there were no seats, I stood.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first as refers to simultaneous events; the second as introduces a reason.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences. First: a text arrived at the precise moment the meeting began; begin "Just as the meeting began". Second: once the meeting finished, you read the text; begin "When the meeting finished".
acceptedAnswers: Just as the meeting began, a text arrived. When the meeting finished, I read the text.
speakingExercises.feedback: Just as highlights precise coincidence; when marks the later action after the meeting.

listeningExercises.audioText: As the audience found their seats, the musicians were tuning their instruments on stage.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was happening while the musicians tuned their instruments?
choices: The audience was leaving the building.
The audience was taking their seats.
The lights had already gone out.
listeningExercises.feedback: As shows that the audience was settling in while the musicians tuned.

listeningExercises.audioText: Just as I pressed Save, the computer shut down without warning.
listeningExercises.prompt: When did the computer shut down?
choices: Before the speaker opened the file.
An hour after the speaker saved.
At the moment the speaker pressed Save.
listeningExercises.feedback: Just as identifies an exact shared moment.

listeningExercises.audioText: As the evening progressed, the traffic gradually became lighter.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word clause heard at the start of the recording, before the comma.
listeningExercises.feedback: As introduces the time frame over which traffic became lighter.

listeningExercises.audioText: As the railway was closed for repairs, we took a bus instead.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the group take the bus?
choices: The railway line was closed for repairs.
They missed the last train by minutes.
They wanted to see more of the town.
listeningExercises.feedback: As means because here; the closure is the stated reason.

listeningExercises.audioText: When I finished packing, I called the taxi. I did not call while I was packing.
listeningExercises.prompt: At what point did the speaker call the taxi?
choices: Halfway through packing.
After finishing the packing.
Before packing began.
listeningExercises.feedback: When marks the finished packing as preceding the taxi call.

listeningExercises.audioText: As I was walking to my interview, it began to rain, so I took shelter.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the speaker doing when the rain started?
choices: Waiting inside the interview room.
Driving away from the interview.
Walking to the interview.
listeningExercises.feedback: As I was walking shows the activity already in progress when rain began.

listeningExercises.audioText: The noise became louder as the train approached the tunnel.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word clause heard immediately after "louder".
listeningExercises.feedback: The as-clause tells us what was happening while the noise increased.

listeningExercises.audioText: The outdoor performance ended just as the storm began.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word phrase heard immediately after "ended".
listeningExercises.feedback: Just as locates the ending at exactly the moment the storm began.
